176.title: Pauri 7, meaning: fame without grace
176.hook: live four ages and be famous everywhere; without His kindly glance, no one asks after you (Japji 7)
176.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the seventh pauri each morning; it is often quoted in talks on humility and on seva done without seeking praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jug, an age, and the sound of pauri seven. Your line was je jug chaare: if your life lasted all four ages, and ten times more. Today, the turn.

The phone lights up, and there's the count. How many people liked the photo. How many read your post. Whether anyone noticed the thing you worked so hard on. It's human to want to be seen, and it can sting when you aren't. Now stretch that as far as it goes: famous everywhere on earth, for age upon age. Guru Nanak's seventh pauri imagines exactly that, and then asks one quiet question about it.
screen: `CHECKING THE NUMBERS.` → `FAMOUS EVERYWHERE, FOREVER.` → `ONE QUIET QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. If your life lasted the four ages, and ten times more; if you were known in all nine regions of the world, and everyone walked along with you; if you kept a good name and won praise and renown across the world: if His kindly glance doesn't fall on you, no one will ask after you. There's the word from pauri four: nadar, the gracious glance. Everything the world admires, long life, fame, followers, a good reputation, is stacked as high as it can go, then weighed against one glance, and the glance is heavier. Then the pauri gets sharper. Without that glance, it says, a person is like a worm among worms, and even wrongdoers point fingers at him. Strong words, but not an insult to anyone; a picture of how small fame really is, in the end. Then a turn toward mercy. Nanak, the One gives virtue to those who have none, and more virtue to the virtuous. And there's no one, the pauri says, who could give Him any virtue in return. So the whole thing flips. Fame is something the world hands out and takes back. Nadar is something only the Giver gives, freely, even to people who have nothing to show. The pauri doesn't call praise wicked; being thanked is lovely. It just says fame isn't it: not the thing that lasts, and not the thing that decides whether anyone asks after you.

Now let the leaning go, sit back, imagine no one ever finds out how good that thing was, and see what's left; maybe there's still something good in it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

177.title: Pauri 8, sound: suniai
177.tomorrow: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening
177.howItsDone: Pauris eight to eleven of Japji, each line beginning suniai, are part of the morning recitation; together they are Japji's stretch on listening to the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar, and the turn of pauri seven: famous for ages, and still, without the glance, no one asks after you. Your line was fame is not it.

If you've ever sat in a gurdwara at dawn while Japji is recited, there's a stretch where one word rolls around and around the room like a wave coming in. It's a soft word, almost a sigh, and once you've heard it you'll hear it all through this part of Japji, because for four pauris straight it starts nearly every line. At the start of this camp, i said Japji would give four whole pauris to one word. Today that word arrives.
screen: `A WAVE COMING IN.` → `A SOFT WORD, ALMOST A SIGH.` → `FOUR PAURIS FOR ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: The word is suniai: SUN-i-ai. The first syllable is like soon, but short, closer to the u in put. Then a light i. Then ai, a little like the start of air. The n in the middle, in Gurmukhi, is the one made with the tongue curled back, the same n you heard at the end of taan in pauri three. Suniai comes from sunnaa, to hear, to listen, and the ending means something like by, or through. By listening. Through hearing. Pauri eight opens: suniai sidh peer sur naath. Sidh: siddhas, yogis said to have gained great powers. Peer: pirs, the Sufi masters, the spiritual guides of Muslim Punjab. Sur: the gods. Naath: the naths, masters of a yogic order; the stories of Guru Nanak's travels have him meeting and talking with them. In one breath, the line names holy people of many kinds from Guru Nanak's world, and says they came to be what they are by listening. Now the rhythm. Pauri eight: suniai, suniai, suniai. Pauris nine, ten and eleven, the same: line after line opening on one soft word, a drumbeat Japji keeps going for four whole pauris. And every one of the four ends on the same two lines, a refrain about devotees being always in bloom. That opens tomorrow.

segments.voice: Say the word slowly, five times, with a breath between each one: suniai. Then stop speaking and do what the word says: listen to the room, the street, your own breath, the small hum of whatever machine is nearby, naming nothing, just receiving it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru be the last sound before the quiet.

178.title: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening
178.hook: by listening one becomes a sage, knows earth and sky, and death cannot touch the devotee (Japji 8)
178.tomorrow: Pauri 9: listening, the gods and scriptures
178.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the eighth pauri each morning; its refrain, that by listening pain and wrongdoing are wiped away, is why listening to Gurbani, in kirtan or katha, is itself treated as practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soft word suniai, by listening, that opens four pauris of Japji. Your line was suniai, listening.

The best listeners aren't always the ones with the best advice. They're the ones who actually stop when someone talks: phone face down, no answer being planned while the other person is still speaking. A conversation like that can feel like being let into a room you forgot you had. Listening like that changes people. Guru Nanak's eighth pauri makes a much bigger claim: listening reaches all the way to earth and sky.
screen: `THE ONE WHO ACTUALLY STOPS.` → `THE PHONE, FACE DOWN.` → `LISTENING REACHES EARTH AND SKY.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening, people become siddhas, pirs, gods and masters of yoga. By listening, the earth, the bull that is said to hold it up, and the sky. By listening, the continents, the worlds and the regions below. By listening, death cannot touch you. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Listening to what? Sikh commentators answer: to the Name, to the shabad, the Guru's word. Suniai isn't just hearing noise; it's taking in the true Name until it rearranges you. Notice how the pauri moves. It starts with holy people, then gets huge: earth, sky, the old picture of the bull beneath the world, whole continents and underworlds. As if listening were no small, private hobby, but how things come to understand their place in everything. Later in Japji, Guru Nanak will gently reinterpret that bull, but that's for another day. Then the pauri comes close again, to one person: poh na sakai kaal, death can't touch you. Kaal is death, and time; the fear of it loses its grip. And the refrain: Naanak bhagtaa sadaa vigaas. Vigaas is the same flower word you met in pauri three, vigsai, blossoming: the devotees are always opening, like flowers. Suniai dookh paap kaa naas: by listening, pain and wrongdoing are destroyed. A big promise for something so quiet, and the same two lines will close each of the next three pauris.

segments.voice: Picture one person you'll talk to today: you're turned toward them, phone face down, listening fully without planning your reply, ready to ask one more question before you say anything about yourself. Then let the picture go and practice on the world, just listening to whatever is here. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

179.title: Pauri 9: listening, the gods and scriptures
179.hook: suniai: by listening even the lowly speak praise, and the scriptures open (Japji 9)
179.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the ninth pauri each morning as part of Japji's four suniai pauris; each ends with the same refrain, that devotees are always in bloom and listening wipes away pain and wrongdoing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suniai: by listening come sages, earth and sky, and death can't touch you. Your line was by listening.

The uncle who complains through every holiday, every single year. The cynic at work who never has a kind word. Then something shifts, a loss, a friendship, maybe just time, and one day a generous sentence comes out of that same mouth. The whole table goes quiet. Where did that come from? This week, pauris nine to fifteen, Japji is about listening and then trusting. And pauri nine, the second listening stanza, has an answer for that uncle.
screen: `THE ONE WHO COMPLAINED.` → `ONE DAY, SOMETHING GENEROUS.` → `WHERE DID THAT COME FROM?`

segments.voice: Pauri nine keeps yesterday's drumbeat, suniai, by listening, at the start of every line. In plain words, following Macauliffe: By listening, Shiva, Brahma and Indra. By listening, even the lowly and the foul-mouthed come to praise. By listening, the ways of yoga and the secrets of the body. By listening, the Shastras, the Smritis and the Vedas. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Shiva, Brahma and Indra are great gods in Hindu tradition, and Guru Nanak names them with respect. The pauri places even their greatness inside listening to the Name. Sikh commentators read it this way: the One is the source, and all greatness, however high, comes by hearing. Then this: suniai mukh saalaahan mand. Mand means the low, the bad; mukh is the mouth. By listening, even those with bad mouths praise. On this reading, nobody is too far gone. Then the body: jog jugat tan bhed, the methods of yoga and the hidden workings of the body. Then the scriptures of Guru Nanak's world: Shastras, Smritis, Vedas. By listening, they open. Their meaning isn't locked in the letters; it comes to the one who listens. Gods, the worst mouth in the room, the body, the books: the pauri says the same thing about each. Whatever is high, whatever is low, the door is listening.

180.title: Pauri 10: listening, truth and contentment
180.hook: suniai: by listening come truth, contentment and wisdom, worth bathing at every shrine (Japji 10)
180.tomorrow: Pauri 11: listening, the blind find the way
180.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the tenth pauri each morning; santokh, contentment, is often taught as one of five virtues, with sat (truth), daya (compassion), nimrata (humility) and pyaar (love).

segments.voice: Yesterday, mand, the low: by listening, even the bad-mouthed turn to praise. Your line was the lowly speak praise.

You're scrolling past a jacket, a phone, a trip, and you already have one that works perfectly well. Still there's a little tug: but this one's better. The tug never quite goes away; there's always a next one. Then there are the rare moments it stops. A meal with friends where nobody checks the time. A quiet evening when nothing is missing. Pauri ten has a name for that feeling, and says where it comes from.
screen: `BUT THIS ONE'S BETTER.` → `THE TUG THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `WHEN NOTHING IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Here is pauri ten in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening come truth, contentment and divine knowledge. By listening, the bath at the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. By listening, reading and reading, honor is won. By listening, the mind settles easily into meditation. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. The heart of it is the first line: suniai sat santokh giaan. Sat is truth, the same root as sach. Giaan is knowledge, wisdom. And in the middle, today's word: santokh. Contentment. Enough. Not giving up, not pretending not to want anything: the settled feeling of having enough, the tug gone quiet. Sikh teaching often counts santokh among the great virtues, alongside truth, compassion, humility and love. And the pauri says it comes from listening. Not from getting the next thing, and not from grimly denying yourself, but from hearing the Name until the restless wanting loosens its grip on its own. Then the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. Indian tradition counted sixty-eight great bathing places, and people walked for months to reach them. Pauri six said the bath is only worth it if it pleases Him. Here Guru Nanak says it plainly: listening is the bath at all sixty-eight at once. And last before the refrain: sahaj dhiaan. Sahaj is ease, naturalness: the meditation that comes without forcing. You don't have to wrestle the tug down. You listen, and it quiets.

181.title: Pauri 11: listening, the blind find the way
181.hook: suniai: by listening the blind find the path and the unfathomable becomes clear (Japji 11)
181.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning as part of Nitnem; Pauri 11 is the last of the four stanzas that begin suniai, by listening, and each of those four ends with the same refrain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, santokh, contentment, the sense of enough that comes by listening. Your line was enough, by listening. Today, the last of the four listening stanzas.

The power goes out at night. The screen dies, the room goes black, and for a second you're lost in your own home. Then you start listening. The fridge is silent, so the kitchen is there. The clock ticks on the left. A car passes, so the window is ahead. Without planning to, you've made a map out of sound, and you find the door. Someone who lives without sight may do this with far more skill, reading a street by its echoes. After three stanzas of suniai, by listening, Japji reaches for that picture: finding your way in the dark.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `A MAP MADE OF SOUND.` → `SUNIAI, ONE LAST TIME.`

segments.voice: Pauri 11 is the fourth and last of the suniai stanzas, a string of short lines each starting with the same word. Its central line, in Guru Nanak's own words: suniai andhe paavahi raahu. By listening, the blind find the road. Around it, in paraphrase: by listening, a person dives deep into oceans of virtue. By listening, ordinary people become like the shaikhs, the pirs and the kings. And by listening, what was fathomless comes within your hand. The word there is asagaah, water too deep to wade across. Listening doesn't drain the ocean. It puts the far shore in reach. So who are the blind? Sikh commentators read this as a blindness anyone can have: not knowing which way to go, stumbling around in our own ego. It isn't a promise about eyes, and it isn't a remark about people who can't see. It's the power cut again: when you can't see the way, you can still hear it. Hear what? In Japji, the Name and the Guru's word, the shabad. The listening is what turns into direction. Then the stanza closes like the other three, for the last time in a while: Nanak says the devotees are always in bloom, and by listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Four stanzas, one lesson. Before you can trust, before you can walk, you listen.

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the sounds arrive, without naming them at first. Then let them slowly make a map: what's near, what's far, what's to your left, what's behind you, how much of the room you can find without looking. If a thought pulls you away, come back by finding where one sound is coming from.
Asagaah. Fathomless, water too deep to wade across: by listening, it comes within reach, and the blind find the road.

182.title: Pauri 12, sound: mannai
182.hook: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae
182.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; pauris 12 to 15 each begin with mannai, and the move from suniai, listening, to mannai, trusting, is often taught as steps on one path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asagaah: by listening, the fathomless comes within reach, and the blind find the way. That closed a week of ears. After Pauri 7, fame is not it, came four suniai stanzas: the power of listening, the lowly singing praise, santokh, enough, and the blind finding the way. Today, a new word takes over.

Your friend says, get some sleep. You hear it. And you stay up anyway. Hearing advice and taking it are two different things. Hearing is the first step; something else has to happen for the words to move in. Japji knows this. Today it changes its word.
screen: `A WEEK OF LISTENING.` → `HEARING ADVICE, TAKING IT.` → `A NEW WORD.`

segments.voice: The new word is mannai. Say it with the n held a moment: MUN-nai. It comes from the Punjabi verb mannanaa, and that verb is wide: to accept, to agree, to obey, to believe, to trust, to take something to heart. When a Punjabi mother tells a child, gall mann lai, she means take my word, go along with it. In Japji, mannai means by trusting, by taking the Word to heart. For the next four stanzas, pauris 12 to 15, line after line begins with it, the way the last four began with suniai. Here's the first line of Pauri 12 in the original: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae. Mannai kee, of the one who trusts. Gat, the state, the condition someone is in. Kahee na jaae, cannot be told. The state of the one who trusts cannot be put into words. Hear the rhythm: mannai kee gat, three quick beats, then kahee na jaae, slowing down, as if the sentence itself runs out of breath. Tomorrow, what it means. Today is for the sound. And notice the order Guru Nanak chose: first suniai, listening, then mannai, trusting. One way Sikh teachers describe the path: you hear the Word, then you take it in, then you live it. A word goes in the ear, then it goes home.
screen: `MANNAI — BY TRUSTING.` · `ACCEPT, OBEY, TAKE TO HEART.` · `MANNAI KEE GAT KAHEE NA JAAE.` · `FIRST LISTEN, THEN TRUST.` · then, large: `MANNAI.`

segments.voice: Say mannai slowly, five times, each on a full breath out: MUN-nai, hold the n, then let the ending open. Rest in the quiet for a few breaths between each. If it helps, let the word sit beside one thing you've heard and haven't yet taken to heart.
Mannai. By trusting, by taking the Word to heart. It opens line after line of pauris 12 to 15, after four stanzas of listening.
Your line: mannai, trusting. For the next four stanzas, it leads the way. Until tomorrow.
